children: Rising Treasury yields are squeezing stock valuations and creating new winners and losers across the market, but Goldman Sachs strategists expect strong corporate earnings and healthy balance sheets to keep the bull market intact.
The 10-year Treasury
yield surged to nearly 5% this week, its highest level since October 2023, while the 30-year yield

climbed to 5.3%, a level not seen in almost 20 years. Goldman economists expect the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark rate by 25 basis points at its next meeting following a hotter-than-expected inflation report.

Strategist Ben Snider attributed the rise in longer-term yields to a combination of higher oil prices, solid economic growth, heavy artificial intelligence investment and expectations for tighter Fed policy.

For investors, the report suggests that the speed of the bond-market selloff may pose a greater immediate threat to stocks than the absolute level of yields. Companies tied to housing appear especially vulnerable, while financial stocks may benefit. Goldman also sees earnings growth as the market’s best defense against further valuation pressure.
Valuations fall as bond yields rise
The S&P 500’s (

) forward price-to-earnings ratio has declined to 19 from 22 at the beginning of the year. Despite that compression, the index remains within 2% of its record high, reflecting the support provided by corporate profits.
Stocks also have not become dramatically more expensive relative to bonds. The difference between the S&P 500 (

) earnings yield and the inflation-adjusted 10-year Treasury yield, a rough measure of the additional return investors demand for owning stocks, stands at about 2.7 percentage points. Goldman said that gap has remained fairly stable during the past two years.

The relationship indicates that higher bond yields have already been reflected partly through lower equity multiples. Further gains for the market may therefore depend more heavily on earnings growth than on investors agreeing to pay higher prices for each dollar of profit.
Fed hikes can produce an early stumble
History points to some near-term turbulence when the Fed begins raising rates. The S&P 500 posted an average three-month return of negative 2% around the start of seven tightening cycles since 1988.
The longer-term record is less alarming. The index generated an average 12-month return of 9% following the first increase, with 2022 the only negative episode in the group.
Goldman noted that markets already price more than three quarter-point rate increases by the middle of 2027. That creates a relatively high hurdle for the Fed to deliver a hawkish surprise.

Past sector performance provides less of a road map. Energy and technology produced the strongest average returns during the first three months after a rate increase, while healthcare was the weakest. However, no sector consistently led or lagged in every cycle.
The speed of the selloff matters
Equities are more sensitive to longer-term yields because much of their value depends on profits expected many years from now. Goldman estimates that roughly 75% to 80% of the S&P 500’s (
) present value comes from cash flows more than a decade into the future.
That helps explain why rapidly rising real yields, which are adjusted for inflation, can be particularly damaging to valuations.

Stocks historically have absorbed moderate increases in yields without major trouble. They tend to struggle when the move becomes unusually sharp. Goldman estimates that a two-standard-deviation increase in the 10-year yield would currently equal approximately 40 to 50 basis points in one month, or around 30 basis points in two weeks.
The recent pace of the increase therefore may explain some of the market’s difficulty, even if investors ultimately conclude that higher rates reflect continued economic strength.
Corporate debt is not yet flashing red

Higher borrowing costs have produced limited damage to large corporate balance sheets so far. Most S&P 500 debt carries fixed rates and relatively long maturities, delaying the impact of higher market yields.

Interest costs also remain manageable compared with corporate profits. Goldman said interest-coverage ratios rank near the top of their historical ranges for the aggregate S&P 500 and remain above average for the median company.

Smaller companies are more exposed because they tend to have weaker balance sheets and a greater proportion of floating-rate debt. Their interest expenses can reset more quickly as benchmark rates rise.
Homebuilders face pressure while financials gain

Housing-related stocks offer one of the market’s clearest expressions of a view on long-term interest rates. Home-construction shares have underperformed the equal-weighted S&P 500 by 16 percentage points since June as higher mortgage rates threaten affordability and demand.

High-growth companies with little current profit also face valuation pressure because much of their expected cash flow lies far in the future. That makes them “long-duration” stocks, meaning their present value is particularly sensitive to changes in discount rates.

Financial companies typically sit on the other side of the trade. Their earnings and stock prices have tended to improve as rates rise, although the benefit can disappear if tighter policy causes credit losses or a significant economic slowdown.
Growth becomes the market’s escape route
Goldman estimates that a company would need to increase its expected long-term growth rate by about 2 percentage points to completely offset a 1-point increase in its cost of equity.

That calculation helps explain the continued corporate spending boom in AI. About half of S&P 500 companies discussed adopting the technology to improve productivity during the latest earnings season, while others are seeking new sources of AI-related revenue.

Companies also are pursuing acquisitions to accelerate growth. Announced U.S. merger volume has reached $1.4 trillion this year, while global activity is up 36% from a year earlier. Goldman said persistently high rates also could encourage more businesses to spin off slower-growing divisions.

The firm separately rebalanced its baskets of long- and short-duration stocks. The broader message is more important than the individual constituents: If yields remain elevated, investors may demand tangible earnings and near-term cash flow rather than distant promises.

title: Goldman Sachs sees rate shock, not bull-market killer, for U.S. stocks
